author_response_spans.text: ## **Reply to the comments from Reviewer #1**

The article entitled: “Supramolecular Pastes: Unlocking Host-Guest Dynamics within Reconfigurable Networks to Modulate Phase Transitions” presents a smart strategy to generate a thermo-reversible paste-to-gel polymer composite by modulating hydrogen bonding through the introduction of trianglamine (TA) into the system. This addition enhances the interaction with clay, thereby reducing the interactions between PNIPAM and clay, which in turn leads to a reversible transition between a paste and a gel according to the temperature. Although the study introduces some innovative concepts, several important details and explanations are missing, which weakens the study.
## Reply

We sincerely thank the reviewer for recognizing the innovative concept of our work and for the constructive feedback. We have thoroughly revised the manuscript to incorporate additional experimental data, mechanistic explanations, and clearer structural insights as requested. We hope these improvements adequately address your concerns and significantly enhance the rigor and clarity of our study.
## **Major points to address:**

1. Only one formulation has been tested, limiting the material study and preventing a meaningful comparative analysis to optimize the system’s behavior. Additionally, there is no indication of the initial polymerization concentration nor of the hydration level of the hydrogel during the self-healing or reprocessability studies, both of which are crucial factors influencing these properties. The impact of varying hydration levels on the material’s behavior should therefore be discussed.
We thank the reviewer for this insightful and constructive comment.

In fact, we used a representative formulation consisting of _1.13 g NIPAM (10 wt%), 0.38 g clay (3.4 wt%), and 0.05 g trianglamine (TA, 0.45 wt%) in 10 g deionized water, yielding a total solid content of 13.85 wt%. This condition was selected based on initial screening, as it demonstrated an optimal balance between mechanical integrity, paste reconfigurability, and thermoresponsive behavior_ . This description was added to the manuscript on Page 6-7 (Highlighted).

To address the reviewer’s concern, we have now conducted a series of systematic comparative experiments with variable clay and TA contents while keeping NIPAM constant. The complete formulation table is presented in Supplementary Table S1, including seven distinct compositions (Ref, C1–C2, T1–T2, CT1–CT2).

_Supplementary Table 1. Detailed formulation of PNIPAM–Clay–TA composite systems used for compositional optimization. NIPAM concentration was fixed at 10 wt% (1.13 g per 10 mL solution), while clay and TA concentrations were varied to study their impact on mechanical, rheological properties of the paste–gel material._

Rheological tests and morphological observations were performed on all samples, and the results are shown in Supplementary Figure 4. These findings demonstrate clear and interpretable trends: (1) Increasing clay content enhances rigidity and G′ (C2, CT2), but reduces flowability and reprocessability; (2) Increasing TA content lowers G′ (T2, CT1), softens the network, and enhances dynamic reconfigurability; (3) Dual extremes (e.g., CT1: low clay + high TA) result in highly flowable but structurally weak pastes, while CT2 (high clay + low TA) yields stiff but brittle materials.

_Supplementary Fig. 4 Morphological and rheological comparison of PNIPAM–Clay–TA paste systems with varied clay and TA content._

These results confirm that the ternary supramolecular system can be finely tuned by compositional parameters, offering a broad design space for application-specific properties. All the above results have been discussed in the revised manuscript (Page 6-7) to clearly describe these results.

Regarding the hydration level: we clarify that all self-healing and reprocessability tests were conducted using the paste materials directly after synthesis, without any additional hydration or soaking steps. These samples retained the intrinsic water content incorporated during the in situ polymerization process and were stored at ambient conditions. No external drying or rehydration was applied prior to testing. Therefore, the observed mechanical behavior and dynamic performance reflect the native hydration state of the synthesized material. We also note that partial dehydration of the paste—such as from prolonged air exposure—leads to noticeably decreased flowability and reduced interfacial healing. This observation highlights the critical role of water in maintaining the dynamic, supramolecular interactions within the network. This condition and its relevance have now been clarified in the revised Experimental Section of self-healing part. (Highlighted on Page 28 and 31).
2. The introduction could be expanded to include related systems, such as dynamic vitrimer materials and reversible/self-healing hydrogels (e.g., involving nanoparticles or proteins).
Reply
We thank the reviewer for this good suggestion. Accordingly, we have included a broader overview of dynamic and reconfigurable materials (Highlighted in the Introduction part on Page 3):
(1) Vitrimers, which rely on associative dynamic covalent bonds to enable reprocessability and self-healing under thermal or chemical stimuli;
(2) Reversible hydrogels involving dynamic interactions between nanoparticles (e.g., silica, nanoclays, or graphene derivatives) and polymers, which impart structural adaptability and self-healing;
(3) Protein-based supramolecular gels, which mimic biological systems and offer reversible binding motifs for reconfigurable soft matter.

We also cite relevant recent works that have inspired our approach in developing a competitive supramolecular interaction framework for paste–gel transformation. The updated introduction now better contextualizes our supramolecular paste design within the evolving field of dynamic soft materials.

3. Could you provide further explanation regarding Supporting Movie 4, which shows material destruction that does not exhibit paste-like behavior? Could this be related to the importance of hydration?

We thank the reviewer for this observation and are glad to share more details concerning Supplementary Movie 4. This video was to demonstrate the significant mechanical differences between the materials under different temperatures. To ensure uniform and rapid temperature exposure, the samples were quickly immersed in hot and cold water, respectively.

However, as shown in this video, the material did not exhibit the characteristic paste-like behavior because it was still immersed in water. The paste-like behavior of the PNIPAM-Clay-TA system relies on a dynamic supramolecular network stabilized by moderately bound water and competitive host–guest interactions. When immersed in water, the system becomes overhydrated and surrounded by excess free water, which disrupts interfacial adhesion and masks the internal viscoelastic characteristics of the paste. In contrast, when the material is removed from hot water and exposed to ambient air, it reverts to its original viscous, moldable paste form within several minutes (Fig. 2 and 3). It is important to note that the paste-like behavior of the PNIPAM-Clay-TA system is highly sensitive to environmental conditions, particularly hydration level and medium of exposure. When the material is immersed in water, its surface interactions and viscoelastic response are masked by the surrounding aqueous phase, making it difficult to observe the intrinsic paste-like rheological features. In contrast, when the material is removed from water and briefly exposed to air, the supramolecular network reorganizes rapidly, recovering its characteristic moldability and stickiness.
4. Mechanical properties (compression or traction) are missing and would provide valuable insight into the gel behavior of PNIPAM-Clay-TA and PNIPAM-Clay systems.
We thank the reviewer for this excellent suggestion.

We would like to clarify that uniaxial tensile testing of the PNIPAM–Clay hydrogel was performed and included in the original SI as Figure S1 (Supplementary Fig. 2 in the revised Supplementary Information). The hydrogel, with its stable network structure and sufficient elasticity, allowed us to obtain meaningful tensile data and assess its mechanical integrity.

However, in the case of the PNIPAM–Clay–TA paste, tensile testing could not be performed due to its intrinsically soft, flowable nature. This material lacks the mechanical cohesion required to support conventional traction or compression tests in its native state. Even in the gel phase induced by heating (above LCST), the material quickly transitions back to the paste state when returned to room temperature—making it incompatible with standard tensile testing protocols, which require structural stability during loading.

Instead, to assess and compare the mechanical behavior of both materials, we performed systematic rheological tests, including time sweeps, amplitude sweeps, temperature sweeps, and cyclic strain tests, which provide robust insight into stiffness, viscoelasticity, and thermal responsiveness. We believe that these rheological measurements are particularly well-suited to characterize soft, supramolecular systems with phase-switchable behavior such as ours.
5. The study lacks an investigation of the PNIPAM-TA system without clay, which would be necessary for a comparative analysis of the different gel properties.
We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion.

In response, we have conducted a comparative study of the PNIPAM–TA system without clay, and the results are now included in the revised Supplementary Information (Supplementary Fig. 3). As shown in the optical image and dynamic rheology measurements, the PNIPAM–TA system without clay forms a low-viscosity, freely flowing solution that lacks any self-supporting or paste-like behavior. The storage modulus (G') remains negligible, confirming the absence of a cohesive network.
**==> picture [527 x 224] intentionally omitted <==**

_**Supplementary Fig. 3.** Comparison of the PNIPAM–TA system with and without clay. (a) Time sweep rheological analysis of PNIPAM–TA with/without Clay. (b) Photograph of the PNIPAM–Clay–TA paste exhibiting a self-standing and moldable form. (c) Photograph of the PNIPAM–TA solution without clay, displaying a fully fluid, non-moldable state._

These findings underscore the critical role of clay as a physical crosslinker that anchors the dynamic host–guest network. Without clay, the TA–PNIPAM interactions alone are insufficient to maintain structural integrity. In contrast, the ternary PNIPAM–Clay–TA system forms a robust, moldable, and thermoresponsive paste, owing to competitive supramolecular interactions among all three components.

We have added these results to the Supporting Information and included a discussion in the manuscript (Highlighted on Page 6) to clarify the compositional rationale and the essential role of clay in the material’s mechanical and phasetransition behavior.
6. In Figures S3, S6, and S7, it is unclear whether PNIPAM-TA pastes include clay. To be consistent, experiments with substitute molecules should also be tested in the presence of clay.
We thank the reviewer for highlighting this important clarification.

We confirm that all samples shown in Figures S3, S6, and S7 in the original SI were prepared in the presence of clay, including the PNIPAM-TA pastes and the systems modified with small molecule substitutes. The omission of “with clay” in the figure legends may cause this confusion and misunderstanding. Therefore, we have now revised the figure captions of Figures S3, S6, and S7 in the original version (Supplementary Fig.6, 10 ,11 in the revised version) to clearly state that the tested materials include clay.

Additionally, we ensured that all other comparative systems were also tested under the same conditions, i.e., with clay present, for a fair and consistent comparison, and we have updated the figure labels and captions accordingly to avoid any confusion.

7. The approach relies on hydrogen bond quenching to impair gelation while maintaining structural stability and a pastelike state. However, simpler H-bond quenchers (such as urea, or else) could potentially achieve similar effects. Could an appropriate concentration of such molecules yield comparable results?

We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. In fact, the more precise description of the role of TA is a powerful competitor here: a stronger hydrogen bond former to reconstruct the entire hydrogen bond network. TA does not only quench/disrupt the original hydrogen bond donor/acceptor, but more importantly outcompete and build up the hydrogen bond sites in the system. Specifically. The incorporation of trianglamine (TA) plays a multifunctional role in the system:
1. Dynamic competition: TA forms strong host–guest interactions not only with PNIPAM but also with clay (as shown by DFT and MD simulations), which outcompete the native PNIPAM–Clay hydrogen bonds.

2. Electrostatic bridging: The protonated amine groups (-NH ₂⁺ ) of TA enable highly strong electrostatic attraction to negatively charged clay surfaces, promoting ordered aggregation and controlled disruption rather than random collapse.

3. Network reconfigurability: Unlike small-molecule quenchers like urea that tend to fully dissolve the network, TA enables a reversible, structured transformation to a moldable paste while preserving sufficient crosslinking density for mechanical integrity and self-healing.
4. Cavity-based supramolecular design: The macrocyclic cavity of TA offers a confined space for dynamic, directional host–guest interactions, which cannot be mimicked by non-specific small molecules.

To further validate this point, we tested the effect of urea in the PNIPAM–Clay system. As expected, urea disrupts gel formation entirely, yielding a fluid solution without any paste-like behavior or network cohesion. This supports the idea that TA enables a fundamentally different and more controllable supramolecular modulation strategy.
**==> picture [527 x 140] intentionally omitted <==**

_Supplementary Fig. 9 The structure of the small molecule urea and fluid liquid state of PNIPAM-Clay-Urea system._ We have added this result to the Manuscript (Highlighted on Page 14-15) the Supporting Information in _Supplementary Fig. 9_ .
8. Additionally, the role of the pH is not discussed, which represents a notable omission.

We thank the reviewer for highlighting the importance of pH in our system. In fact, the TA is prepared by adding excess conc. HCl to fully protonated its precursor trianglamine to obtain trianglamine▪6HCl salt with good aqueous solubility. The pH of its aqueous solution is concentration dependent, typically ranging from 3~5. Thus, the supramolecular architecture of our system depends critically on the protonation state of trianglamine (TA), which directly influences its solubility, hydrogen-bonding capacity, and distribution within the composite network.

Our standard formulation is depicted in Material and Methods part ( _1.13 g of purified NIPAM monomer is dissolved in 10 mL deionized water containing a dispersion of 0.38 g of "Laponite XLG" nano clay and 0.05 g of TA macrocycles_ ), which ensures that TA is fully protonated and thereby remains could be well dissolved in the aqueous system (neutral tranglamine or tranlamine in basic condition shows poor aqueous solubility). In this concentration, TA aqueous solution shows a pH ~ 3 (we do not use buffer or additional acid/base to adjust the pH), This protonated form of TA in  acidic condition actively participates in hydrogen bonding with both PNIPAM chains and the clay surface, enabling the formation of a homogeneous and reconfigurable supramolecular paste.

Accordingly, we added a discussion about the pH and solubility (Highlighted on Page 5): _The host macrocycle TA with protonated amine -NH2[+] groups, which is prepared by adding excess conc. HCl aqueous solution and dissolved well in deionized water (pH ~ 3), could interact strongly with both the clay and PNIPAM polymer chains._
9. Is it necessary to polymerize NIPAM in situ? Could similar results be achieved by simply mixing PNIPAM, clay, and TA?
We thank the reviewer for raising this important question.

To address this point, we conducted a control experiment by directly mixing pre-synthesized PNIPAM (commercially obtained), clay, and trianglamine (TA) in water at the same concentrations used in our in situ polymerization system. The resulting mixture failed to form a homogeneous or stable supramolecular paste. As shown in the figure below, the
three components could not be uniformly integrated, and the mixture separated into distinct phases with visible aggregation and poor cohesion.

In contrast, the in situ polymerization of NIPAM in the presence of both clay and TA allows for the gradual integration of monomers, supramolecular hosts, and crosslinking interactions into a single coherent and reconfigurable network. This process appears to be essential for forming a uniform dynamic paste with tunable rheology and reversible paste–gel transitions. We believe that the stepwise molecular assembly during polymerization is critical for establishing intimate hydrogen bonding and host–guest interactions that cannot be reproduced through simple blending.

**Figure.** Control experiment of simply mixing pre-synthesized PNIPAM, clay, and TA without in situ polymerization. The mixture fails to form a homogeneous paste and shows poor miscibility and phase separation. The image shows distinct aggregate formation and non-uniform dispersion.

10. In Figure 5d, an irreversible strain is indeed observed during the first cycle, although it remains relatively consistent. However, subsequent cycles show stable reversibility, with even better G' compared to the PNIPAM-Clay-TA system. This appears contradictory to the claims made and should be clarified.
We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful and important comment.

We acknowledge that in Figure 5d, the PNIPAM–Clay hydrogel exhibits an initially irreversible drop in G′ during the first strain cycle, followed by apparently stable and repeatable behavior in subsequent cycles. However, we would like to emphasize that this should not be interpreted as evidence of self-healing or true structural reversibility.

The G′ recovery observed after the first cycle is most likely the result of network densification and mechanical stiffening, caused by irreversible rearrangement of hydrogen-bonded domains under strain. After this "pre-compaction" event, the system enters a metastable state that is mechanically resilient, but not dynamically reconfigurable. The apparent reproducibility of G′ in later cycles reflects a static mechanical stabilization, not a supramolecular self-healing process. In contrast, the PNIPAM–Clay–TA paste demonstrates true self-healing behavior, as shown by its ability to rejoin and reflow across damaged or separated interfaces at rest, a phenomenon driven by dynamic host–guest and hydrogen bond interactions. This clear distinction highlights the benefit of TA incorporation in constructing a dynamically reconfigurable network.
Thanks to the reviewer’s suggestion to improve the interpretation of this figure, we have now added clarification to this effect in the revised manuscript (Highlighted on Page 20):

_In contrast, the PNIPAM-Clay hydrogel exhibits a clear decline in both storage and loss modulus after the first high-_ – _strain deformation (Fig. 5d), indicating irreversible structural disruption. Although the PNIPAM Clay hydrogel shows stable G_ ′ _recovery after the first loading cycle, this behavior arises from mechanical consolidation rather than true supramolecular healing. This plateau does not signify dynamic recovery. Instead, it reflects the mechanical response of a partially collapsed, non-reconfigurable network that lacks supramolecular reversibility._
**==> picture [527 x 32] intentionally omitted <==**
11. Similarly, Figure 6b appears counterintuitive compared to Figure 5d, which shows potential self-healing behavior based on rheological data.
We thank the reviewer for this meticulous observation.

The apparent contradiction arises from the different nature of the two experiments. Figure 5d presents a cyclic strain rheology test, where the PNIPAM-Clay hydrogel is subjected to repeated alternating low and high strains. While the G' values appear stable in the later cycles, this reflects a mechanically arrested state, as discussed previously, rather than true dynamic self-healing. The network has already undergone irreversible collapse after the first cycle and cannot recover its original structure.

In contrast, Figure 6b shows a macroscopic self-healing experiment based on cut-and-contact recovery. In this test, the hydrogel is physically severed, and the two pieces are brought back into contact under ambient conditions. The fact that the PNIPAM-Clay hydrogel does not restore its mechanical integrity in this setup further confirms that it lacks the dynamic supramolecular interactions required for true self-healing.

In fact, Figure 5d presents a bulk rheological assessment of the entire cut sample and does not capture localized behavior at the cutting interface. In contrast, Figure 6b provides direct visual evidence of the failure to self-heal at the cut surface. Together, these figures offer complementary insights, and when interpreted appropriately, they are fully consistent. Notably, only the PNIPAM–Clay–TA paste exhibits both cyclic rheological recovery and macroscopic selfhealing, attributable to its dynamic host–guest supramolecular network.

12. Conductivity tests would be more relevant and justified if their significance were better explained, as the presence of water in the gel and paste already contributes to conductivity. Therefore, the addition of GO is questionable. What happens to the conductivity without GO?

We thank the reviewer for this valuable question. While pure water possesses an extremely low intrinsic conductivity due to the absence of free charge carriers, the addition of electrolytes can enhance ionic conduction. However, in semisolid systems such as gels or pastes, ion mobility is significantly restricted by the confined polymer network, resulting in limited overall conductivity. Therefore, the incorporation of conductive fillers such as graphene is necessary to establish percolated electron-conducting pathways and achieve meaningful conductivity in the composite material.

To address and prove this point, we performed a control experiment using the PNIPAM–Clay–TA paste without any added graphene. As shown in the following figure, the resulting material was unable to light up a small LED bulb, confirming that ionic conductivity from the paste alone is insufficient for functional electronic applications in this system. In contrast, when graphene was incorporated, the paste successfully conducted electricity and enabled LED illumination (as demonstrated in Figure 6a and Supplementary Movie 8).
**==> picture [144 x 169] intentionally omitted <==**

This clearly indicates that the addition of graphene is essential to create a continuous electronic conduction pathway across the material. The conductive behavior cannot be achieved through water-mediated ionic transport alone. These results support the functional necessity of graphene in our conductive demonstration.

In addition to demonstrating the necessity of graphene for achieving conductivity, we would like to emphasize that the primary purpose of this demonstration is to highlight the versatility of the PNIPAM–Clay–TA paste as a dynamic supramolecular platform. The paste itself exhibits excellent moldability, thermal responsiveness, and structural integrity.

By incorporating functional fillers such as graphene, we are able to extend its utility into electronic applications, such as the soft, flexible circuit shown in our demonstration. This concept is not limited to conductivity. We envision the supramolecular paste as a tunable base material that can be customized by incorporating other functional nanomaterials: Magnetic nanoparticles could impart magneto-responsiveness for remote actuation; Photonic or plasmonic particles could provide optical sensing or light-modulation capabilities; Bioactive or catalytic components could expand its utility into biomedical or chemical sensing applications. Thus, this work presents a generalizable design framework, where host–guest driven supramolecular pastes serve as a responsive, reconfigurable platform for multi-functional materials development.
We thank the reviewer for giving us the opportunity to further elaborate on the broader potential of our system.
## **Minor revisions:**
1. In Schemes 1b and 1e, the different networks are not clearly described. The colors (blue, yellow, red spheres) should be explicitly indicated in the legend.
We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion.
We revised Figure 1a, 1b and 1e with updated the figure legends to clearly define the meaning of each element.

2. It is unclear what specific information the IR analysis provides, as both PNIPAM gel and PNIPAM-Clay-TA show similar spectra, where no significant differences in peak sharpness at 1550 and 1650 cm-1 are observed. As a suggestion, a Raman analysis in the hydrated state might provide more qualitative and quantitative insights into interaction differences.
We thank the reviewer for this insightful observation about the FTIR analysis and constructive suggestion about the Raman analysis.

However, we respectfully point out that FTIR spectra in hydrogen-bonded soft materials often show only subtle changes when interactions are distributed across a network and when hydrogen-bond acceptors/donors are present in small quantities. In our system, TA was added at ~0.45 wt%, which is deliberately low to act as a structural modulator rather than a dominant matrix component. Therefore, we do not expect sharp new IR bands, but rather collective, distributed shifts, particularly in band widths or background features.

However, we conducted a new set of FTIR measurements of freshly freeze dried PNIPAM–Clay and PNIPAM–Clay–TA and also NIPAM monomer, PNIPAM polymer, Clay, TA (as shown in Supplementary Fig. 5a-5b). Firstly, as shown in FTIR, the spectra of PNIPAM–Clay gel and PNIPAM-Clay-TA paste confirm successful polymerization of NIPAM, evidenced by: i) the disappearance of characteristic vinyl C=C (stretching, 1618 cm[-1] ) and =CH2 bands (out-of-plane bending, 962 and 708 cm[-1] ); ii) shift amide C=O stretching peak from 1655 cm[-1] of NIPAM to 1635 cm[-1] of PNIPAM, gel and paste; iii) weaken C-N stretching peak at 1244 cm[-1] . Secondly, by adding TA, obviously, a small new shoulder appears near 2350 cm ⁻ ¹ in the PNIPAM–Clay–TA sample, which is absent in the clay-only or PNIPAM–Clay gel controls. This may indicate an altered supramolecular environment or the formation of TA involving strong supramolecular interactions, which accords well with the appearance of 2000 cm-1 in Raman analysis. Besides, in the C-N stretch region near 1250 cm ⁻ ¹, a slight shift of this peak is observed in the PNIPAM–Clay–TA paste sample (1250 cm-1) compared to those of PNIPAM–Clay gel (1257 cm-1) and TA (1215 cm-1) samples, suggesting that TA may interact strongly with the clay and PNIPAM, consistent with their dynamic interactions in this ternary system.

Moreover, according to the reviewer’s helpful suggestion, we also conducted Raman spectroscopy under hydrated conditions, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 5c. Most notably, we observe a broad, paste-specific Raman band centered around ~2000 cm ⁻ ¹, which is completely absent in TA, Clay, and the binary PNIPAM–Clay gel. This band is attributed to new supramolecular-level interactions, possibly from TA related interactions including strong TA-Clay electrostatic interactions and TA-PNIPAM hydrogen bonds. This Raman signature is indicator of a new physical environment and network topology in the TA-containing paste system, distinguished it from the PNIPAM–Clay gel.

We acknowledge, however, that these spectral changes are subtle, which can be attributed to the relatively low loading of TA in the formulation. This is expected, as the hydrogen-bonding interactions and host–guest inclusion effects are non-covalent and may not always manifest as prominent peak shifts in bulk IR analysis. Nonetheless, these data, taken
together with rheological and morphological evidence, support the conclusion that TA modulates the network structure through supramolecular interactions.

_Supplementary Fig. 5. FTIR and Raman analysis of network structure and interactions._

We have now included these new characterizations in the revised Supplementary Fig. 5, and an explanatory paragraph has been added to the main text (Results section) to guide interpretation (Highlighted on Page 7-8).

3. Traditionnally, a contraction of the material is typically observed in PNIPAM hydrogels above the LCST due to chain collapse. However, such an effect is not apparent in the movies or images. Could the authors confirm this point and provide comments on it?
We thank the reviewer for this careful observation.

It is well known that PNIPAM hydrogels exhibit volume contractions above their LCST due to chain collapse and water expulsion. However, in our PNIPAM–Clay–TA system, the observed paste-to-gel transition occurs almost instantaneously upon heating and is accompanied by a rapid network stiffening, rather than a gradual dehydration process. Importantly, during our experimental demonstrations and video recordings, we focused on capturing the immediate morphological and mechanical change at the moment of thermal triggering.

While molecular-scale PNIPAM chain collapse happens rapidly, macroscopic volume shrinkage in composite hydrogel systems typically requires additional time (several minutes) due to the slow diffusion of water. In our case, the bulk water content of the material remains largely unchanged during the initial paste-to-gel transition, and no visible contraction is observed in the short time window of measurement. If the gel is maintained at elevated temperature for a prolonged period, water loss and volume reduction do occur, as expected. However, this effect is not captured in our standard experimental timeframe.
4. Traditionally, increasing temperature disrupts hydrogen bonds. What would happen if the temperature were raised significantly above 40 °C? Could higher temperatures lead to any side effects? Reply

We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful question. As correctly noted, increasing temperature can disrupt hydrogen bonds. In our system, this thermally induced hydrogen bond weakening is a key design feature that underlies the reversible phase transition from a supramolecular paste to a physically crosslinked gel. Upon heating above the lower critical

solution temperature (LCST) of PNIPAM (~32 °C), the hydrophobic collapse of PNIPAM chains, coupled with reduced hydrogen bonding between the polymer and clay/TA, leads to the formation of a more rigid, load-bearing gel network. This process is fully reversible.

To evaluate the thermal stability and reversibility of this transition, we conducted cyclic rheological tests between 25 °C and 55 °C (Fig. 2d-e), well beyond the LCST range. The results clearly demonstrate that the material undergoes a reversible increase and decrease in storage modulus (G') across temperature cycles, with no signs of mechanical degradation, hysteresis, or phase instability. Importantly, no irreversible side effects such as aggregation, or chemical decomposition were observed under these conditions.

Therefore, our findings confirm that the reversible paste–gel transition remains robust even under elevated temperatures (up to 55 °C), and the system maintains its structural integrity and functional responsiveness without adverse thermal side effects.

5. The following sentence on p15 is not intuitive: "This indicates that the BTA with larger intrinsic capacity has a weaker effect on the gel formation, resulting in a more rigid semi-solid gel rather than semi-liquid paste." Could the authors explain why a weaker interaction would lead to a more rigid, semi-solid gel?

We thank the reviewer for raising this important question. As discussed, without TA (no strong TA related interactions), PNIPAM-Clay produce semi-solid hydrogel; With TA (with strong TA related interactions), PNIPAM-Clay-TA create semi-liquid paste. In this regard, the BTA with ‘a weaker interaction’ (modest BTA related interactions) may lead to a state between the gel and paste, which is termed as a more rigid, semi-solid gel here.

In order to make this clearer, we revise this sentence to: _This indicates that the BTA with larger intrinsic capacity, in stark contrast to TA with strong hydrogen bonding effect to produce paste, has a weaker effect on the paste formation, resulting in a more rigid semi-solid gel rather than semi-liquid paste._ (Highlighted on Page 18-19)

6. Scheme 5g does not provide additional information. As a suggestion, more detailed scheme illustrating the network structures at 40 °C (before and after self-healing, with van der Waals interactions) compared to the network at 32 °C (with hydrogen bonding interactions) would be more insightful.

We thank the reviewer for raising this important question. In fact, Figure 5g is mainly drawn to highlight the self-healing details, particularly the components and supramolecular interactions involved for the self-healing process at room temperature. We have revised Figure 5g to make the damage part, and hydrogen bonding interactions (Blue dashed line) in self-healing part clearer for understanding.
## Reply

We sincerely thank the reviewer for the positive and encouraging evaluation of our manuscript. We are pleased that you found our work on the thermo-responsive supramolecular paste–gel system to be innovative and promising for the development of smart materials. We have carefully addressed all your specific comments and suggestions, which significantly helped us improve the clarity and completeness of the manuscript. Below, we provide a detailed point-bypoint response and highlight all revisions in the manuscript using yellow highlights.
1. Authors can add subheadings in the result and discussion section to enhance the structure and readability of the manuscript.
We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion.

To improve the logical flow and accessibility of the manuscript, we have revised the Results section by introducing clear subheadings (Highlighted in the Manuscript). These subheadings highlight the key aspects of the study, including:
## Material design and synthesis;
Comparative rheological analysis of the hydrogel and paste;
Temperature-triggered reversible paste–gel transition;
Reversible shape reconfiguration and programmability;
Molecular simulations and supramolecular mechanism;
Self-healing performance;
Self-healing electrical circuit demonstration.
We believe these additions enhance the clarity and navigability of the manuscript.
2. Structural information of materials is not provided in the main text figures. The authors should add structural characterization data of the materials in the main text figures.

We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. We have added the Materials and Methods sections with detailed structural characterization data of the materials in the Manuscript. Additionally, Figure 1 was revised with detailed legend description and Laponite XLG information.
3. The manuscript does not clearly describe the impact of clay and TA content on hydrogel. It is necessary to provide mechanical property data for hydrogels with varying clay and TA contents.

We thank the reviewer for this important observation. To clarify the influence of component concentrations on the mechanical properties of the supramolecular hydrogel system, we have conducted a series of comparative experiments with variable clay (2.0–5.0 wt%) and TA (0.2–1.0 wt%) contents, while keeping NIPAM concentration fixed at 10 wt%. The full formulation table is presented in Supplementary Table S1.

_Supplementary Table 1. Detailed formulation of PNIPAM–Clay–TA composite systems used for compositional optimization. NIPAM concentration was fixed at 10 wt% (1.13 g per 10 mL solution), while clay and TA concentrations were varied to study their impact on mechanical, rheological properties of the paste–gel material._

Mechanical performance was evaluated via rheological testing. As shown in Supplementary Figure 4, the storage modulus (G′) varied significantly with composition. Samples with higher clay content (e.g., C2 and CT2) exhibited greater stiffness and higher G′ values, but reduced flowability and moldability. In contrast, higher TA content (e.g., T2 and CT1) resulted in lower G′ values and more deformable paste behavior, suggesting that TA modulates hydrogen bonding and introduces network mobility through supramolecular competition.
**==> picture [240 x 227] intentionally omitted <==**
_Supplementary Fig. 4. Morphological and rheological comparison of PNIPAM–Clay–TA paste systems with varied clay and TA content._

These results demonstrate that both clay and TA content can be used to fine-tune the material’s mechanical response. This compositional tunability offers design flexibility depending on the target application, whether improved mechanical integrity or enhanced reconfigurability is desired. We have added a corresponding paragraph in the revised manuscript (Highlighted on page 6-7) to clearly describe these results.
4. The manuscript does not provide the FTIR spectra of TA and clay. The authors should provide a more detailed discussion of the FTIR spectra to explain the formation of hydrogen bonds.

We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion. Accordingly, we performed new FTIR measurements on freshly synthesized samples of all relevant components, including NIPAM monomer, PNIPAM polymer, nano clay, TA, and their binary and ternary composites. These data are now presented in Supplementary Fig. 5a-5b.

This transition in our system is not merely a result of thermal responsiveness but is deeply rooted in the dynamic supramolecular interactions among PNIPAM, Laponite clay nanosheets, and the protonated trianglamine (TA) macrocycles.

At the core of this behavior lies the well-known lower critical solution temperature (LCST) of PNIPAM (~32 °C). Below this temperature, PNIPAM chains are hydrated, expanded, and interact extensively with both TA and clay via hydrogen bonding. These multivalent, non-covalent interactions form a loosely crosslinked and highly dynamic network, resulting in a paste-like material with flowability and plasticity. The inclusion of TA plays a critical role in this state: it disrupts the relatively stronger PNIPAM–clay hydrogen bonds and introduces dynamic host–guest interactions, effectively reducing crosslinking density and promoting a deformable, moldable matrix.

As the temperature increases above the LCST, PNIPAM undergoes a hydrophilic-to-hydrophobic shift, leading to chain collapse and dehydration. This thermally triggered conformational change diminishes hydrogen bonding with TA and clay, while simultaneously promoting stronger hydrophobic interactions and van der Waals forces. These interactions drive tighter association between PNIPAM chains and clay surfaces, leading to increased crosslinking density, mechanical stiffness, and structural integrity. ## Designing supramolecular pastes by – controlling host guest dynamics in recon figurable networks 

Received: 6 April 2025 Accepted: 7 August 2025 Check for updates 

Jinrong Wang[1,3] , Weibin Lin 1,3, Valeriia O. Nikolaeva1, Rukhma Javaid1 & Niveen M. Khashab 1,2 

Stimuli-responsive phase transitions endow smart systems with adaptive functionalities, yet reversible paste-to-gel transitions remain largely unexplored. Here, we report a protonated trianglamine (TA)-based supramolecular — – paste, in which competitive supramolecular interactions host guest binding — – – and electrostatic forces drive the formation of a dynamic TA clay polymer ternary network with paste-like rheology. The material exhibits reversible paste-to-gel transitions under mild thermal stimuli, enabling shape reprogramming, temperature-triggered self-healing, and shape fixation. DFT calculations and molecular simulations reveal the molecular basis of the – host guest interactions in guiding network dynamics and healing behavior. Furthermore, incorporating graphene as conductive filler renders the paste functions as a stretchable, self-healing conductive wire, with potential in flexible electronics and responsive devices. This work introduces supramolecular pastes as a versatile class of smart materials that go beyond traditional hydrogels in structural adaptability and multifunctionality. 

The design and development of smart materials with adaptive and responsive properties have garnered significant attention in the field of soft matter and supramolecular chemistry[1][–][8] . Among these, supramolecular hydrogels have emerged as an exciting class of smart materials, offering a combination of dynamic responsiveness, adaptability, and structural versatility[9][–][13] .

Unlike traditional chemically crosslinked hydrogels, supramolecular hydrogels rely on non-covalent interactions such as hydrogen bonding[14] , π-π stacking[15] , hydrophobic forces[16] . as well as host-guest complexation[17] . These reversible and tunable interactions endow them with features, including self-healing, stimuli-responsiveness, and the ability to mimic natural dynamic systems[18][–][22] . Consequently, supramolecular hydrogels have found applications across diverse domains such as controlled drug delivery[23][,][24] , tissue engineering[25][,][26] , soft robotics[27][,][28] , and sensing[29][,][30] , positioning themselves as a cornerstone for next-generation smart soft materials. 

Recent advances in dynamic polymer networks have also led to the development of vitrimer systems, which utilize associative exchange reactions within covalent adaptable networks to achieve thermally re-processable, recyclable, and self-healing materials[31] . These materials demonstrate excellent shape programmability and mechanical recoverability through bond-exchange mechanisms, and represent a covalent counterpart to the non-covalent design principles explored here. In parallel, nanocomposite hydrogels integrating inorganic nanoparticles have shown enhanced mechanical strength and self-healing through dynamic physical interactions[32][,][33] . These systems often exploit reversible hydrogen bonding, electrostatic interactions, or π–π stacking to create energy-dissipative and reconfigurable networks. Moreover, protein-based supramolecular hydrogels, inspired by biological scaffolds, employ reversible non-covalent motifs such as β-sheet formation, metal coordination, or host–guest interactions to achieve responsiveness and dynamic remodeling[34][,][35] .

However, research on the paste-to-gel phase transition remains scarce[40] , and a significant challenge lies in designing smart materials that exhibit reversible transitions between a semi-solid gel and a semi-liquid paste. 

Engineering dynamic and competitive supramolecular interactions that can respond to and adapt to external stimuli offers a promising strategy[41][–][44] . This requires the careful design of dynamic crosslinking, as well as competitive and cooperative interactions through multiple associative and dissociative mechanisms[3] . Macrocycles, with their intrinsic cavities and guest-binding properties, are ideal candidates for the precise control of complex formation via various reversible and competitive host–guest interactions[45][–][49] .

Incorporating macrocycle-based host–guest complexes into semisolid hydrogels can enhance processability, impart tunable properties, and broaden their potential applications. Nevertheless, to the best of our knowledge, the role of host-guest interactions and their competitive supramolecular interactions in paste-to-gel phase transition have never been studied before. 

In this study, we report the reversible transition between a semisolid gel and a semi-liquid paste by introducing host trianglamine (TA) macrocycles into the PNIPAM hydrogel system. The incorporation of TA establishes specific competitive host-guest interactions and a dynamically controllable crosslinking pattern among the host macrocycle (TA), guest polymer chains (PNIPAM), and clay, resulting in a semi-liquid ‘hydropaste’ state that is distinct from traditional liquid solution and semi-solid gel. This supramolecular viscous paste displays a suite of features, including injectability, the ability to freely mold into any shape, and a reversible paste-to-gel transformation triggered by temperature changes. Unlike conventional hydrogels, this material boasts exceptional self-healing capabilities due to the strong and reversible binding affinity of TA. The dynamic crosslinking network, governed by the locked and unlocked states induced by TA, supports repeated and reversible remodeling cycles, enabling high adaptability and reconfigurability. Through density functional theory (DFT) calculations and molecular simulations, we elucidate the molecular mechanism by which TA enhances the formation of this supramolecular paste and enables its self-healing functionality.

These findings underscore the transformative role of macrocyclic compounds in creating dynamic, reconfigurable networks within supramolecular systems. By enabling a reversible paste-to-gel transition, this approach opens previously unexplored pathways for the development of smart materials with adaptability, self-healing, and shape-reprogrammable properties—capabilities that remain challenging to achieve with conventional hydrogel systems.

The PNIPAM-Clay hydrogel was synthesized via free radical polymerization at room temperature (25 °C) overnight (Fig. 1a). Laponite XLG clay served as the physical cross-linker, facilitating interactions with the PNIPAM chains through hydrogen bonds formed between the amide side groups of the polymer chains and the surface functional groups of the clay, such as –OH and Si–O–Si units (Supplementary Fig. 1)[50] . The clay’s abundant hydrogen bonding sites effectively anchor the polymer chains, restricting their mobility and rendering them immobilized (Fig. 1b)[51] . The resulting hydrogel exhibited a robust, semi-solid state with impressive mechanical properties, as depicted in Fig. 1c, Supplementary Fig. 2, and Supplementary Movie 1. Upon freeze-drying, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) revealed a well- 

defined, honeycomb-like porous structure with nanoscale pores ranging from 500 to 600 nm (Fig. 1d). 

Upon incorporating host TA macrocycle into the pre-gel solution prior to free radical polymerization and allowing the reaction to proceed overnight (Fig. 1a), a significant transformation was observed.

HCl aqueous solution and dissolved well in deionized water (pH ~3), could interact strongly with both the + clay and PNIPAM polymer chains. Specifically, the -NH2 groups on TA compete with clay for hydrogen-bonding sites while simultaneously forming hydrogen bonds with the amide groups of PNIPAM. Additionally, strong electrostatic interactions occur between the positively charged TA and the negatively charged clay, leading to aggregate formation and further modifying the network structure. These competitive host-guest interactions reduce the fixed hydrogen-bonding sites that anchor PNIPAM to the clay, increasing the mobility and flexibility of PNIPAM chains (Fig. 1e). Instead of forming the previously described semi-solid hydrogel structure, the incorporation of host TA yielded a viscous, paste-like material with a noticeable degree of fluidity (Fig. 1f and Supplementary Movie 1). To further dissect the role of each component in the supramolecular network, we compared the PNIPAM–TA system without clay. The clay acts as a physical crosslinker that not only contributes mechanical rigidity but also mediates competitive binding interactions with both PNIPAM and TA, enabling the formation of a cohesive, moldable, and thermoresponsive supramolecular paste.

Samples with both low clay and high TA content (CT1) exhibited the lowest modulus and highest flowability, while those with high clay and low TA (CT2) showed the highest stiffness but were brittle and less moldable. ## Self-healing performance 

The smart PNIPAM-Clay-TA paste, in contrast to the PNIPAM-Clay hydrogel, exhibits good self-healing capabilities, as demonstrated through comprehensive cyclic strain time sweep rheology tests (Fig. 5a–c). For the paste, both the storage modulus (G’) and the loss modulus (G”) show a decreasing trend with increasing strain, eventually equalizing around 65% strain (Fig. 1i). The strain time sweep rheology of the PNIPAM-Clay-TA paste (Fig.

5a) indicates that at low strain (0.1%), G’ > G” characterizes a gel-like state. However, under high strain (100%), the paste transitions to a sol state (G’ < G”). Self-healing ability is further evaluated through continuous cyclic strain tests (0.1% strain → 100% strain → 0.1% strain) at a constant angular frequency (10 rad s[−][1] ) and 25 °C. As shown in Fig. 5b, c, applying a 100% strain shifts the paste into a sol state (G’ < G” and tan δ > 1). When the strain is reduced back to 0.1%, the paste rapidly reverts to the original state (G’ > G” and tan δ < 1), with G’ and G” values swiftly recovering to their initial levels without any loss. The self-healing behavior is consistently observed across cyclic tests, with moduli nearly returning to their original values over successive strain cycles. These highlight the temporary disruption of cross-linking in the paste network under high strain, followed by its quick, reversible restoration under low strain. The paste’s ability to autonomously self-heal within seconds opens possibilities for applications that demand materials with dynamic, selfhealing responsive properties. In parallel, similar cyclic tests were performed on the PNIPAM-Clayhydrogel. In contrast, the PNIPAM-Clay hydrogel exhibits a clear decline in both storage and loss modulus after the first high-strain deformation (Fig. 5d), indicating irreversible structural disruption. Although the PNIPAM–Clay hydrogel shows stable G′ recovery after the first loading cycle, this behavior arises from mechanical consolidation rather than true supramolecular healing. This plateau does not signify dynamic recovery. Instead, it reflects the mechanical response of a partially collapsed, non-reconfigurable network that lacks supramolecular reversibility.

The macroscopic self-healing capability of the PNIPAM-Clay-TA paste is vividly illustrated in Fig. 5e. The paste was deliberately cut into two separate pieces, and when the cut surfaces were brought into contact at 25 °C, they seamlessly merged and healed within seconds, requiring no external intervention. Conversely, the same test with the PNIPAM-Clay hydrogel showed that even after hours, visible cracks remained between the sections (Fig. 5f), revealing its limited selfhealing capacity. This comparison clearly highlights the enhanced selfhealing capabilities of the smart paste, making it a highly advantageous material for applications that require durability and self-healing. 

The swift self-healing mechanism of this paste hinges on a dynamic and reconfigurable network founded on reversible intermolecular hydrogen bonding, as elucidated in Fig. 5g. The introduction of host TA with host-guest interactions into the paste system plays a dual role. (Remarks to the Author)

The article entitled : « Supramolecular Pastes: Unlocking Host-Guest Dynamics within Reconfigurable Networks to Modulate Phase Transitions » presents a smart strategy to generate a thermo-reversible paste-to-gel polymer composite by modulating hydrogen bonding through the introduction of trianglamine (TA) into the system. This addition enhances the interaction with clay, thereby reducing the interactions between PNIPAM and clay, which in turn leads to a reversible transition between a paste and a gel according to the temperature. Although the study introduces some innovative concepts, several important details and explanations are missing, which weakens the study.
Major points to address:

1. Only one formulation has been tested, limiting the material study and preventing a meaningful comparative analysis to optimize the system’s behavior. Additionally, there is no indication of the initial polymerization concentration nor of the hydration level of the hydrogel during the self-healing or reprocessability studies, both of which are crucial factors influencing these properties. The impact of varying hydration levels on the material’s behavior should therefore be discussed.
2. The introduction could be expanded to include related systems, such as dynamic vitrimer materials and reversible/selfhealing hydrogels (e.g., involving nanoparticles or proteins).

3. Could you provide further explanation regarding Supporting Movie 4, which shows material destruction that does not exhibit paste-like behavior? Could this be related to the importance of hydration?
4. Mechanical properties (compression or traction) are missing and would provide valuable insight into the gel behavior of PNIPAM-Clay-TA and PNIPAM-Clay systems.

5. The study lacks an investigation of the PNIPAM-TA system without clay, which would be necessary for a comparative analysis of the different gel properties. 6. In Figures S3, S6, and S7, it is unclear whether PNIPAM-TA pastes include clay. To be consistent, experiments with substitute molecules should also be tested in the presence of clay.

7. The approach relies on hydrogen bond quenching to impair gelation while maintaining structural stability and a paste-like state. However, simpler H-bond quenchers (such as urea, or else) could potentially achieve similar effects. Could an appropriate concentration of such molecules yield comparable results?
8. Additionally, the role of the pH is not discussed, which represents a notable omission.

9. Is it necessary to polymerize NIPAM in situ? Could similar results be achieved by simply mixing PNIPAM, clay, and TA? 10. In Figure 5d, an irreversible strain is indeed observed during the first cycle, although it remains relatively consistent. However, subsequent cycles show stable reversibility, with even better G' compared to the PNIPAM-Clay-TA system. This appears contradictory to the claims made and should be clarified. 11. Similarly, Figure 6b appears counterintuitive compared to Figure 5d, which shows potential self-healing behavior based on rheological data. 12. Conductivity tests would be more relevant and justified if their significance were better explained, as the presence of water in the gel and paste already contributes to conductivity. Therefore, the addition of GO is questionable. What happens to the conductivity without GO?
## Minor revisions:
1. In Schemes 1b and 1e, the different networks are not clearly described. The colors (blue, yellow, red spheres) should be explicitly indicated in the legend.

2. It is unclear what specific information the IR analysis provides, as both PNIPAM gel and PNIPAM-Clay-TA show similar spectra, where no significant differences in peak sharpness at 1550 and 1650 cm-1 are observed. As a suggestion, a Raman analysis in the hydrated state might provide more qualitative and quantitative insights into interaction differences. 3. Traditionnally, a contraction of the material is typically observed in PNIPAM hydrogels above the LCST due to chain collapse. However, such an effect is not apparent in the movies or images. Could the authors confirm this point and provide comments on it?
4. Traditionally, increasing temperature disrupts hydrogen bonds. What would happen if the temperature were raised significantly above 40 °C? Could higher temperatures lead to any side effects?
5. The following sentence on p15 is not intuitive:
"This indicates that the BTA with larger intrinsic capacity has a weaker effect on the gel formation, resulting in a more rigid semi-solid gel rather than semi-liquid paste."
Could the authors explain why a weaker interaction would lead to a more rigid, semi-solid gel?

6. Scheme 5g does not provide additional information. As a suggestion, more detailed scheme illustrating the network structures at 40 °C (before and after self-healing, with van der Waals interactions) compared to the network at 32 °C (with hydrogen bonding interactions) would be more insightful.
## Reviewer #2
## (Remarks to the Author)

In this paper, the authors report a PNIPAM hydrogel system within trianglamine (TA) and Laponite XLG. In this hydrogel system, the competing interactions between clay, TA, and host polymer can be regulated by controlling the environmental temperature, resulting in the reversible phase transitions between paste and gel. Based on this flexible phase transitions property, the hydrogel exhibits self-healing and free deformation characteristics in its paste form and can solidifies upon heating. This approach opens new pathways for the development of smart materials. The manuscript can be considered for publication after the following revision.
1. Authors can add subheadings in the result and discussion section to enhance the structure and readability of the manuscript.
2. Structural information of materials is not provided in the main text figures. The authors should add structural characterization data of the materials in the main text figures.
3. The manuscript does not clearly describe the impact of clay and TA content on hydrogel. It is necessary to provide mechanical property data for hydrogels with varying clay and TA contents.
4. The manuscript does not provide the FTIR spectra of TA and clay. The authors should provide a more detailed discussion of the FTIR spectra to explain the formation of hydrogen bonds.
5. The manuscript lacks further explanation of the internal mechanisms during the gel phase transition. More structural characterization data is needed to investigate this mechanism.
6. The supplementary videos are very big, please compress them to small files for easy communicating.
7. This related reference (Small, 2024, 20(43), 2404231) based on macrocycle-PAM hydrogels can be cited.
## Reviewer #3
## (Remarks to the Author)

In the manuscript entitled “Supramolecular Pastes: Unlocking Host-Guest Dynamics within Reconfigurable Networks to Modulate Phase Transitions”, the authors incorporated host macrocycles (trianglamine, TA) during the polymerization of N- isopropylacrylamide (NIPAM) with nano clay resulted in the successful transformation of the initially PNIPAM-clay gel into a viscous supramolecular PNIPAM-clay-TA paste. The smart viscous supramolecular paste has a temperature triggered paste to gel reversible transition due to the hydrophobic interaction of PNIPAM with clay and TA.Furthermore,the PNIPAM-clay-TA paste demonstrated a rapid self-healing recovery. Additionally, by incorporating conductive fillers such as graphene, we demonstrate the use of this material in self-healing conductive wires.However, several issues need to be addressed before the manuscript would be reconsidered for publication.

1.In the abstract, the authors stated “the incorporation of host macrocycles (trianglamine, TA) during the polymerization of N isopropylacrylamide (NIPAM) resulted in the successful transformation of the initially PNIPAM gel into a viscous supramolecular paste”.Actually,PNIPAM gel should be PNIPAM-clay gel formed through the hydrogen bond interaction between PNIPAM and clay.Moreover,the TA in the PNIPAM-clay-TA system leads to a viscous supramolecular paste due to the proper size of TA cavity and host-guest interaction. Some statements need to be clarified.

2.In order to understand the effect of the proper cavity of TA on the formation of the PNIPAM-clay-TA paste,the authors discussed the effect of the larger cavity of BTA on PNIPAM-clay-BTA system and concluded the larger cavity of BTA leading to the formation of a semi gel. If possible, the authors would investigate if a smaller cavity of macrocycles would lead to formation of PNIPAM-clay-macrocycles paste or not.
- 3.The PNIPAM chain is physically crosslinked by hydrogen bond of the nano clay surface. The chemical structure of the nano clay should be clearly illustrated in Figure 1(a)

4.Although the fabrication of the PNIPAM-clay hydrogel and PNIPAM-Clay-TA paste is described in the Supporting Information, the solid content or concentration of the PNIPAM-clay and PNIPAM-Clay-TA paste is not clear.Because the concentration significantly affects rheological properties and mechanical properties of the paste and gel, the authors should clarify the specific concentration of every sample.

5.In this article, the polymerization is carried out at 25°C for 20 hours. Usually,a free radical polymerization of NIPAM can be completed for 4 or 5 hours. Why is the polymerization completed for 20 hours. Furthermore, the polymerization of NIPAM at 25°C could result in the phase transition of PNIPAM chains due to a fast increase of temperature caused by the exothermic free radical polymerization.Usually,the polymerization of NIPAM is carried out at 0oC ice water to form a homogeneous PNIPAM solution.
6.The size distribution of the Clay has two peaks, while the size distribution of Clay and TA only has one peak. The data seem unreasonable.
7.In the Supporting information, PNIPAM hydrogel and PNIPAM-TA paste should be corrected into PNIPAM-Clay hydrogel and PNIPAM-Clay-TA paste in all Figures and captions of the Figures.
